-122.39400,37.79180.name: Reproductive Medicine Associates of Northern California
-122.39400,37.79180.desc: A fertility clinic reporting to the CDC's National ART Surveillance System. Medical director: Scott Morin, MD. A fertility clinic is where human embryos are made, selected and stored, and where assisted reproduction happens, like IVF, ICSI, egg and sperm donation, freezing embryos and eggs for later. Reporting is required of every US clinic performing assisted reproduction, under the Fertility Clinic Success Rate and Certification Act, so this is close to a complete register rather than a list of members. What it records is cycles started, which is not the same as children born.

6.08021,49.56510.name: BioneXt
6.08021,49.56510.desc: A clinic mapped in OpenStreetMap as offering fertility treatment. OpenStreetMap holds what somebody chose to map, so a country with few points here may be thinly mapped rather than thinly served. That is the reverse of the national registers alongside it, which are close to complete for one country and silent everywhere else. This layer is a cross-check and a source of leads, not a count.

77.45870,28.77500.name: Dabur Research Foundation
77.45870,28.77500.desc: An organisation accredited by AAALAC International for its care and use of laboratory animals. Part of Dabur India Limited. Accreditation is voluntary and paid for, so this is a list of organisations that chose to be inspected rather than a register of everyone doing the work. An organisation absent from it is not accredited; that says nothing about whether it uses animals. In several countries the largest users are absent for exactly that reason. The directory gives a city and country and no street address, so this point marks where the organisation is registered rather than the building where animals are held.

-84.67000,37.67000.name: Lexington VA Health Care System
-84.67000,37.67000.type: Animal Welfare Act veterans affairs hospital
-84.67000,37.67000.desc: Veterans Affairs hospital registered with USDA APHIS under the Animal Welfare Act, certificate 61-V-0003. This is the address on the registration. A research registration is issued to an organisation rather than to a building, so for a university it is usually the research administration office and the animals are elsewhere on campus or in another city. Rats, mice and birds bred for research are excluded from the Act's definition of an animal — the overwhelming majority of animals used, and the great majority of the genetically altered ones. What is covered here is dogs, cats, primates, rabbits, guinea pigs, hamsters and farm animals. The rest is counted nowhere.

-87.62723,41.83142.name: IIT Research Institute
-87.62723,41.83142.state: 10 West 35th Street Chicago, IL 60616, United States
-87.62723,41.83142.desc: A BSL3+ laboratory, operational. Run by Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT). It is categorised as a private laboratory, working on human health. It stands in a built-up area, with more than fifty thousand people living within two and a half miles. There is no international register of laboratories at this containment level and no obligation to declare one, so this record comes from a research project rather than a regulator. What that project could not find out is absent here too.

-9.13930,38.72230.name: Direção-Geral de Alimentação e Veterinária
-9.13930,38.72230.desc: Portugal’s agriculture authority, overseeing the EU’s second and much smaller area of engineered maize. Portugal and Spain together are essentially the whole of EU cultivation, and both require coexistence measures and public registers of planted fields.

10.74000,59.92000.name: Norwegian Biotechnology Advisory Board
10.74000,59.92000.desc: Norway’s public advisory body on biotechnology, which runs open consultations and publishes reasoned positions including on gene drives and germline editing. It is the clearest working example of a country building deliberation into biotechnology policy rather than adding it afterwards.

9.70000,52.40000.name: Bundessortenamt — variety registration
9.70000,52.40000.desc: Before a variety can be sold in the EU it must be registered as distinct, uniform and stable. Uniformity is the requirement that quietly excludes the diverse populations smallholders and organic growers prefer, so a technical seed-marketing rule written for industrial agriculture decides what may lawfully be sold, entirely separately from any biosafety question.

-81.97480,33.47350.name: Xytex Corporation
-81.97480,33.47350.desc: A US sperm bank, and the defendant in the litigation that established how little of a donor profile is checked. Families who selected one donor were told he held degrees, had a very high measured IQ and was pursuing a doctorate, and that the company screened donors by reviewing family health history and criminal records and conducting interviews and physical examinations. Much of the self-reported profile had not been verified. The donor's sperm was distributed for more than a decade and at least 36 children were born from it. Two structural facts sit underneath the case. Nobody regulates or records how often a donor may donate in the United States: this company set its own ceiling, reported as sixty families per donor. And when families sued, courts repeatedly treated the claims as wrongful birth and dismissed them, until the Georgia Supreme Court allowed several to proceed in 2020 — including a claim under the state's fair business practices law that the bank had misrepresented its screening to the public. That is the distinction this facet turns on: not whether a child should have been born, but whether a company sold a service it did not perform.

-122.48530,37.85910.name: Genetic Savings & Clone
-122.48530,37.85910.desc: The first commercial pet cloning company, opened in 2000 with more than ten million dollars from a single backer, and closed at the end of 2006 having told clients it could not develop the technology to the point where cloning pets was commercially viable. Its record is precise and instructive: it funded the first cloned cat, produced five cloned cats in all, and sold two, the first for a reported $50,000 before the price was cut to $32,000. It never cloned a dog, which was the founder's original purpose. Alongside the cloning it ran a tissue bank, charging several hundred clients an annual fee to store material against a future clone — a service sold years before the service it was for could be delivered. The pet tissue banks operating today are the same proposition, and this is the case where the second half never arrived and the fees were refunded.
